That's okay! I'm glad you're asking!

Genderqueer/Genderfluid: Your gender does not feel male or female, so you identify as genderqueer. Genderfluid is switching in between genders, or a mix or genders, depending on how you feel. They are very similar but some prefer one term over the other.

Agender- someone does not feel like they have a gender, so they identify as agender.

Accepting these gender terms requires an understanding that gender is not binary male or female), and that it is not determined by your biological characteristics (which are not 100% male or 100% female anyway)

Pansexual- you can be sexually attracted to a person of any gender. Like being bisexual, except you can be attracted to people who are genderqueer or agender as well. Also, some bisexuals are not attracted to transgender people (depending on the person I guess), and pansexual covers that too.

Demisexual- you can only be attracted to people that you have a strong emotional connection with. People like to write it off as "normal attraction" but it is closer to asexual. Within being demisexual, you can have any romantic orientation (who you would have a relationship with/who you can be attracted to after the emotional connection happens).

For example, I identify as panromantic demisexual, meaning I can be attracted to any gender after (and as long as) I have an emotional connection to them.

I hope this helped, if you have more questions feel free to ask! :)

GNS3, VIRL, IOU, and others and lots of time going through different lab scenarios and familiarizing yourself with different protocols will take you a long way in general networking.

Look at some of the entry level cert books from the networking vendors. Get a subscription to safaribooks if you don't want to pay 60 bucks a pop for a book. I'm still on an old 10/month plan with 5 slots that I think you can still get if you call them. When you're going through those, don't just read the books. Go through the scenarios they pose in your own lab. Play around and break things and figure out how to fix them again. That's how you'll start really understanding what the authors are telling you.

Then of course there are different disciplines within networking like data center, SP, and wireless which you can get into after you've established the fundamentals.

There is of course no substitute for real world experience on real world problems but as long as you don't expect to start at the top that in my opinion is the key to help get you in the door and prepared to do well in a real position.

Well often times you'll do something unintentional that will break functionality. What I mean more specifically though is as you get into a lab, start working on those "I wonder if" scenarios.

What if I change this metric here? What if I want traffic to flow this way instead of this other way? What happens if I use this other flavor of spanning tree on this switch?

You'll really find you gain a deeper understanding of what you thought you already knew from these kinds of scenarios. Keep at it and you'll often find yourself understanding the protocols more deeply than the books explain.

GNS3 and get yourself Wireshark. If you can understand what is happening in a Wireshark TCP session you will have a great foundation for many networking scenarios. Start a simple session, say telnet and walk through every packet in that establishment of the connection. GNS3 is better than having HW, you can take it with you, and you can run labs from the coffee shop. I bought a router to study for my CCNA, CCIP and CCNP exams, but in the end GNS3 was all I used.

Telnet is used when you configure a device that you do not have access to, kind of like remote desktop. Telnet has been replaced (mostly) by SSH, which is kind of like telnet with SSL.

To add to what others are saying, labbing, is the key. I like to use GNS3 and VIRL, which is a bit clunkier somehow, but supports more cisco products. Both are very nice, and these links should help you get an idea of what kinds of labs to do:
